I read 13,900 analytics job postings in Ontario this year. Here is what changed between January and September.

In January, contracts were the exception. One in six postings. By August they were nearly one in three, and they rose in every single role, not just the usual suspects. Business Analyst roles went from one in five contract to one in three. If you have been turning down contracts on principle, the market has quietly moved against that principle.

The second shift is who the market is hiring for. Mid-level roles grew. Senior stayed flat. Junior roles fell to under 3% of all postings, and the few that exist are the most crowded in the dataset: nearly a third of them hit 200+ applicants. Senior roles hit that mark a third as often. The entry door is narrower and the line in front of it is longer.

Third, what the postings actually ask for. SQL is still number one by a wide margin. Then Excel. Then Power BI and Python, neck and neck. Excel still outranks Python in 2026, and the gap did not close this year. What moved up: Agile, data modeling, Azure, Power BI. What moved down: Python, statistics, Tableau, machine learning. The market is asking for people who can model data and work inside a delivery process, more than people who can fit a model.

Which brings up the strangest number in the set. The share of postings that name AI in the role requirements doubled, from one in five to over 40%. The share that list machine learning as a skill fell. Employers want you to use AI. Almost none of them want you to build it. (I excluded the "we use AI to screen applications" disclosures, which Ontario now requires; those alone are another 11%.)

So, if you are hunting an analytics role right now:
Say yes to contracts. They are more than a quarter of the market and less crowded than permanent roles.
Lead with SQL, Excel and Power BI. Python is fourth and slipping.
Add Agile and data modeling to the top of your resume. They are the two fastest growing asks.
Describe how you use AI in your actual work. Not ML. Not models. Tools, workflows, what it saved.

My goodness... I love baseball. 

Nothing is better than high-stakes October baseball.

If you've been following me for a minute, you know I am an Atlanta Braves fan.  Of course, we HAVE to talk about last night.

Ray Kerr. 
Our starting pitcher last night against the Dodgers.

The perfect underdog story.

A former foster kid.  A community college pitcher who quit baseball. He worked in a movie theater and a 7-Eleven.
An undrafted free agent who signed with the Seattle Mariners in 2017 for a modest $2,000 bonus.

He's been out of baseball for the past two years, recovering from Tommy John surgery.

He went head-to-head against Dodgers pitcher Blake Snell--- who makes an average annual salary of $36,400,000 under his current contract. 

The Atlanta Braves won 3 - 2 in a game they never should have won.

---- 

I'm a former recruiter and have interviewed hundreds, if not thousands, of candidates over my career. 

I am also a small business owner and employer. When I hire, I look for grit. I want people who WANT to work. 

They are hungry to learn and desire to win. 

Hiring managers are tired. 

They’re bruised and battered. Over the past decade, leaders have navigated the pandemic, the Great Resignation, and now the AI transformation—often with leaner budgets and smaller teams as businesses restructure and optimize for technology.

They are tired of training new people and worn out from having to pick up the slack.

I hear some version of this from managers over and over: “I just need to find someone who will do their dang job.”

So if you want to impress a hiring manager in an interview, find a way to demonstrate GRIT and initiative.

💼 Assume everyone is understaffed and overwhelmed. 

The hiring manager wants to find someone who can jump in and add value from Week 1.

(Sidebar: Yes, some companies are willing to mentor. Yes, some offer robust training and rotational programs. But even those organizations generally assume you bring a basic skill set to the table.)

When I talk to leaders, there’s a common theme.

Sure, they want the Googliness:
→ Grit
→ Intense curiosity
→ Divergent thinking
→ Collaboration
But they also want GSD.

Get Sh*t Done. ✅

And here’s the thing:
You don’t prove you have GSD by saying you’re a hard worker.

You prove it with evidence.

In your interview, don’t tell me you’re a problem solver. Tell me about a problem you saw that wasn’t technically yours—and what you did about it.

In your one-on-one, don't tell me you’re proactive. Tell me about something you anticipated and fixed before anyone asked.

Don’t tell me you’re resilient. Tell me about a time things went sideways and you figured it out.

The best candidates don’t just tell me what they’re capable of. They give me receipts.

Ray Kerr had every reason to be counted out.

Instead, he took the ball against one of the best teams in baseball and got the job done.

That’s the kind of person I want on my team.

AI can replace the junior marketer. But then who becomes the senior marketer?

Gartner says AI will let high-performing marketing teams "eliminate the traditional bottom rungs of the corporate ladder" by 2030.

So I asked the marketing leaders in the MHQ community: are you still hiring junior marketers?

One head of marketing at a three person AI startup told me, "Claude is literally my intern." Her first junior hire isn't even in her top five.

Nalini Robbins at Smith.ai spent two weeks learning Claude Code, cleaned up 1,797 internal links, rebuilt metadata across 163 pages, and built a workflow that helped increase organic traffic 20%. She also ended an SEO agency contract that had been costing $18K/month.

AI is already doing work people used to spend a lot of time doing. And I think it's awesome. I'm doing tons of it myself. But there's a part that worries me.

Early in my career I made a lot of decks look pretty for executives. Boring work? Absolutely. But I learned which slides survived the meeting, what execs actually cared about, and how they wanted a story told.

That tedious work is where I learned the job.

If AI does that work for the next generation, where do they build the judgment they'll need to eventually lead?

We spent 3 months with a customer’s legal team on what “training” means in an AI contract.

Their template said we couldn’t retain any learning from the engagement. And their definition of learning covered the humans on my team - the engineers who spent months inside their systems were supposed to walk out with nothing in their heads.

Consulting has run on the opposite assumption for a hundred years. McKinsey partners don’t forget banking when they leave a bank engagement. Auditors don’t develop amnesia between clients. Knowledge sticks to people, gets applied to the next project, and everyone treats that as the point of hiring consultants.

Put AI in the vendor name and the same knowledge accumulation reads like a data breach.

The templates most legal teams work from were built for software you licensed or services you billed by the hour. AI vendors don’t slot into either bucket. Language that made sense for one category turns into nonsense when you try to deliver real work under it.

Every buyer wants AI. Every vendor wants to sell them AI. The paperwork between them is stuck in 2018. It's going to take years to catch up. Until then, redlines and patience, I guess.

8+ years in product management. Here's what I wish every aspiring PM knew.

I'm Dedric. From 2020 to 2023 I was a Product Manager at Salesforce, and today I'm a Senior Salesforce Product Manager. Along the way I've earned 9 Salesforce credentials, plus SAFe 6 Product Owner/Product Manager and Certified ScrumMaster.

Here's what product management actually comes down to:

1️⃣ The job is choosing the right problem.
Intake, business cases, prioritization. Most of the real work happens before anything gets built.

2️⃣ The hardest problems usually aren't technical.
In almost every role I've had, it was the same knot: two teams, two systems, no shared truth. Untie that first. Then automate.

3️⃣ Outcomes beat output.
Nobody remembers how many features you shipped. They remember results:
→ 2M+ CRM records migrated with zero downtime
→ SSO and MFA rolled out to 8,000+ users, access incidents down 40%
→ $15M+ in enterprise contract value protected through a platform migration

4️⃣ You can build PM skills before you have the PM title.
Prioritizing, aligning stakeholders, writing acceptance criteria, measuring results after launch. If you do those at work, you're already practicing product.

That's why I built Blazer2Role: a guided path from your current career into a high-paying tech role. Coaching, curriculum and community, built for working professionals.

Human approval is still one of AI’s strongest safeguards.

As AI systems move from generating answers to taking actions, the question is no longer only, “Can AI do this?”

It is also, “Where should a human stay in control?”

Here are 8 places where human-in-the-loop approval matters most:

1. Financial transactions - AI can analyze risk, but payments should still pass a human checkpoint.

2. Customer refunds - Eligibility and fraud checks can be automated, while exceptions need review.

3. Contract decisions - AI can analyze clauses and flag risks, but final changes should remain accountable.

4. Employee decisions - Recommendations can assist, but hiring, promotion, or disciplinary outcomes need human judgment.

5. System access - Permission analysis can be automated, while sensitive access should require approval.

6. Production changes - AI can assess impact and recommend actions, but deployment decisions need oversight.

7. External communications - AI can draft responses, but high-impact messages should be reviewed before release.

8. High-risk exceptions - AI can classify risk and collect evidence, while final action should stay with humans.

The goal is not to slow AI down.

It is to place human judgment exactly where the cost of a wrong action is high.

Good AI governance is not human versus AI.

It is AI handling speed and scale, while humans retain accountability, context, and final authority where it matters most.

How Should You Monetize an AI SaaS Product?
AI SaaS Monetization Series #2

Mistake #2: Charging for Something Customers Don't Understand

So once founders realize AI costs fluctuate, they immediately start looking at internal cost drivers, meaning tokens, API calls, credits, characters processed and similar things.

These metrics are great for your internal spreadsheets because they tell you what the product costs to run, but forcing customers to think in those terms is problematic.
Just imagine hiring an accountant who charges you based on how many keys they hit on their keyboard while typing your tax return.
You would most likely tell them you don't care about their typing. You care about having a completed tax return, therefore, the outcome, nothing else.

AI products work the same way. Customers care about the finished (done) job, like analyzing a prospect, resolving a support ticket, reviewing a contract, or drafting a video script.
If you make buyers guess how many tokens an operation takes, you introduce friction right at the moment of purchase. They can't calculate their ROI, and they end up worrying about hidden costs every time they click a button. That's stressful.
Before you map your pricing to raw technical usage, ask yourself: What unit does the customer actually associate with getting value? And that is your real starting point.

This is part 2 of my series on AI monetization traps.
Up next: outcome-based pricing sounds amazing on paper, but jumping into it too quickly usually backfires.

Observator recently ran a segment on Romanian companies that are "hiring" AI agents, on a monthly subscription rather than an employment contract. Our CEO and co-founder, Cristi Movilă, was one of the founders invited to explain what these agents actually are.

We don’t want to spoil the segment for you, so we’ll keep it short: a chatbot answers, an agent acts. It searches, writes, sends, fills in, and, above all, makes and takes phone calls!

That last part is where we focus most. OptiComm.AI's voice agents don't call at random. They call because our prediction platform already knows that a specific customer will need a specific product, in a specific quantity, in the coming days. The agent turns the prediction into a conversation, and the conversation into an order.

Two data points from the segment are worth keeping in mind:
- Only 5 in 100 Romanian companies use AI, almost four times below the EU average
- EU law requires people to be clearly told when they're talking to an AI system.

The first is an opportunity. The second is a rule we treat as a product standard, not a formality.

Senior QA / Senior Quality Engineer your value is judgment, not execution. 

A Senior QA / Senior Quality Engineer should not simply be a faster version of a QA Engineer.

That is one of the biggest misconceptions in QA career progression.

Being senior does not mean:
Writing more test cases.
Finding more defects.
Automating more scenarios.
Executing regression faster.
Knowing more tools.

Those things can demonstrate experience.
But they are not what makes someone senior.
The real shift is judgment.

A Senior QA should be able to look at a change and ask:
What is the real risk here?
Which customer journeys could be affected?
Where should we test this?

What belongs at unit, integration, API, contract, backend acceptance, or E2E level?
What should be automated?
What is not worth automating?
Which edge cases actually matter?
What evidence do we need before release?
What can we consciously leave untested?
That last question is important.

Seniority is not about trying to test everything.
It is about knowing what deserves the most attention.
A Senior QA should also start seeing patterns that others may miss.
Repeated production defects.
Fragile integrations.
Weak testability.
Missing lower-layer coverage.
Unstable automation.

Poor test data.
Risky architecture decisions.
Gaps in observability.
Patterns across releases.
And then do something with that insight.
Not just report the problem.
Influence how the team solves it.
That means the role also changes from individual execution toward enabling others.
Mentor junior engineers.
Review test approaches.
Challenge assumptions.

Help Engineering improve testability.
Support better automation decisions.
Bring risk into Product discussions.
Improve release confidence.
Help the team learn from incidents.
A strong Senior QA should make the whole team better.
Not become the person who must personally test every difficult feature.
There is another important change at this level.

You start moving from:
“Here is what I tested.”
to:
“Here is what I believe the risk is, here is the evidence, and here is my recommendation.”
That is a very different level of contribution.
Technical depth still matters.

Senior QA / Senior Quality Engineer your value is judgment, not execution. 

A Senior QA / Senior Quality Engineer should not simply be a faster version of a QA Engineer.

That is one of the biggest misconceptions in QA career progression.

Being senior does not mean:
Writing more test cases.
Finding more defects.
Automating more scenarios.
Executing regression faster.
Knowing more tools.

Those things can demonstrate experience.
But they are not what makes someone senior.
The real shift is judgment.

A Senior QA should be able to look at a change and ask:
What is the real risk here?
Which customer journeys could be affected?
Where should we test this?

What belongs at unit, integration, API, contract, backend acceptance, or E2E level?
What should be automated?
What is not worth automating?
Which edge cases actually matter?
What evidence do we need before release?
What can we consciously leave untested?
That last question is important.

Seniority is not about trying to test everything.
It is about knowing what deserves the most attention.
A Senior QA should also start seeing patterns that others may miss.
Repeated production defects.
Fragile integrations.
Weak testability.
Missing lower-layer coverage.
Unstable automation.

Poor test data.
Risky architecture decisions.
Gaps in observability.
Patterns across releases.
And then do something with that insight.
Not just report the problem.
Influence how the team solves it.
That means the role also changes from individual execution toward enabling others.
Mentor junior engineers.
Review test approaches.
Challenge assumptions.

Help Engineering improve testability.
Support better automation decisions.
Bring risk into Product discussions.
Improve release confidence.
Help the team learn from incidents.
A strong Senior QA should make the whole team better.
Not become the person who must personally test every difficult feature.
There is another important change at this level.

You start moving from:
“Here is what I tested.”
to:
“Here is what I believe the risk is, here is the evidence, and here is my recommendation.”
That is a very different level of contribution.
Technical depth still matters.

Accenture's shares opened 22% higher last Thursday, on relief that AI isn't hurting it. On the earnings call, chief executive Julie Sweet said: "We are definitely giving more productivity due to AI."

The relief had reasons. Revenue rose 5% in local currency to $74.2bn. There were 141 client bookings above $100m, twelve more than the year before, and next year's revenue forecast beat expectations. A year ago Accenture said it was exiting people it could not reskill, and it shrank from 791,000 to 779,000 in a single summer. It finished this August at about 814,000.

Keith Bachman of Bank of Montreal asked during the earnings call how much AI was cutting the price when a client renews a contract for the same work. Angie Park, the finance chief, called the impact "steady," without saying how large it was. Sweet was plainer. Accenture is "absolutely giving more AI efficiencies" to clients, she said, and more than making up for it overall with new kinds of work and bigger projects. Separately, she said the fourth quarter brought "lower pricing in many areas of our business." And next year the firm will hire more slowly, "in part due to AI."

So the effect the market stopped fearing is already there, in renewals and in next year's hiring plan. This year, growth paid for it. Revenue per person rose too, and how the saving divides between Accenture and its clients is visible only from inside.

If you renew a services contract this year, Sweet has said on the record that AI efficiency is passed on at renewal.

From our corner of the UK hiring market, Q3 gave us some genuinely useful signals.

Demand broadened across the Pulse Group portfolio.

Product vacancies grew 59% quarter on quarter, Design 55%, and AI & Data 326%. AI & Data was the breakout area by some distance. Technology remains our largest discipline overall, although activity eased slightly from a very strong Q2. 

We worked on hiring projects across Retail & Consumer, Media & Publishing, Education & Research, Energy & Utilities and Financial Services, with AI & Data demand building particularly strongly across Retail and Media. 

In most Product searches, clients are still favouring people who have worked in a closely related industry or product environment.

Square peg, square hole seems to be winning.

That is useful for candidates. Relevance needs to be obvious. Sector knowledge, product context and clear examples of similar problems solved are carrying real weight.

Pay moved as well.

Our median permanent salary increased from £80k in Q1 to around £90k in Q3, with the £80k to £100k band the busiest part of the permanent market for us this year so far. Product carried the highest median salary below leadership at £95k, with AI & Data at around £90k. 

Contract activity strengthened as well, with placements up 150% quarter on quarter, across twice as many clients. Median contractor pay across our book is £500 a day (mainly outside IR35 roles), with Product at £580, AI & Data at £550 and Security at £650. 

Across Pulse, vacancy flow increased 34% from Q1 to Q3, while first interview activity increased 58% over the same period. 

The increase in vacancy flow matters because it has kept pace with our growing team.

The other big theme was conversion.

Our CV-to-interview ratio was just under 2:1, with plenty of searches effectively 1:1. Our vacancy-to-placement ratio is around 2:1 year to date, and 100% with several exclusive clients.

That tells us a tighter brief, deep qualification and commitment to the Pulse process are producing better outcomes.

Dozens of people started new roles through Pulse during Q3, while contractor extensions meant more people continuing in work.

It’s been incredible to see the Pulse Experience in action! Deep discovery and qualification, clear communication and accountability throughout the process are showing up in stronger conversion and better outcomes for our clients.

Our mission stays the same: give everyone we interact with a great experience, regardless of the outcome.

We enter the final stretch of 2026 with plenty of opportunity in front of us.

Let’s go Q4!! 🚀
